issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (e.g., UML: class Stock {...}) but the template repository provides an 'Inventory' class that implements the stock behavior and leaves Stock.java empty. The solution implementation also uses Inventory (SealSaloon.stock is of type Inventory). This mismatch between the expected type name 'Stock' in the specification and the actual type 'Inventory' in the template/solution is a structural inconsistency that will confuse students about which class to implement and which type SealSaloon.stock should have.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the naming consistent across all artifacts. Either: (A) Update the template and solution to provide and use a proper Stock class (implementing the same methods currently in Inventory) and remove/replace Inventory, or (B) Update the problem statement and UML to refer to 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock', and remove the empty Stock.java from the template. Ensure SealSaloon.stock is declared with the same type name as described in the problem statement/UML.

issues.description: The problem statement consistently refers to the stock component/class as 'Stock' (including the UML and required static SealSaloon.stock of type Stock), but both the template and solution code implement and use a class named 'Inventory' for that same concept. This naming divergence (Stock vs Inventory) creates a mapping cognitive burden: students reading the problem will look for a Stock class and Stock-based methods, while the provided code exposes Inventory and its methods, leading to confusion about which class they must modify or use.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the name for the stock concept across all artifacts. Either (A) rename the Inventory class and its file to Stock (and update all references in SealSaloon and elsewhere to use Stock), or (B) update the problem statement and UML to use 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock' so it matches the provided code. Ensure the file names and class names match exactly to avoid student confusion.
